title: start with the person in the mirror
hook: start with the person in the mirror

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: thoughts. Your line: let it pass. Did one loud thought show up sounding very sure of itself? Did you let it pass, even once? Day eight, and week two begins.

Think about the last time a friend messed something up. Missed a deadline, said the wrong thing, burned the dinner. What did you say to them? Probably something like: hey, it happens, you're tired, it's fine. Now think about the last time you messed something up. What did you say to yourself? For a lot of us, the voice inside is one we would never allow anyone to use on a friend. Idiot. Of course you did. Typical. Week two is about how we treat people. And one old tradition insists you start with the person in the mirror. Today's word is kindness.
screen: `WHAT YOU SAY TO A FRIEND.` → `WHAT YOU SAY TO YOURSELF.` → `START WITH THE MIRROR.`

segments.voice: In the early Buddhist teachings there's a word, metta. It's usually translated loving-kindness, but it comes from the Pali word for friend. Metta is friendliness: wanting good for someone the way a friend does. A short discourse called the Metta Sutta describes it with a picture: the way a mother would protect her only child with her own life, a person can grow a heart like that toward every living being, without limit. Here's the surprise. About fifteen hundred years ago, the Buddhist teacher Buddhaghosa wrote a long guide to meditation, and when he explains how to practice metta, he says not to start with everyone. Start with yourself. Wish yourself well first, with phrases like may I be happy, may I be free from trouble. Then, when that feeling is steady, extend it outward: to a friend, to someone neutral, and eventually to someone difficult. His reasoning is simple. It's hard to hand someone a thing you've never held. Remember day four, and the line from Leviticus: "love thy neighbour as thyself." Those last two words carry a quiet assumption, that there's some care for yourself to measure by. And modern research points somewhere similar. The psychologist Kristin Neff has spent years studying what she calls self-compassion: treating your own failures the way you'd treat a friend's. People often worry that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. In her studies and others, it tends to go the other way. People who are gentler with their own mistakes are often more willing to admit them, and more likely to try again. Kindness isn't a reward for getting it right. It's where you start.
screen: `METTA: THE FRIEND WORD.` · `START WITH YOURSELF, THEN OUTWARD.` · `AS THYSELF.` · `GENTLE WITH MISTAKES, MORE LIKELY TO TRY.` · then, large: `KINDNESS IS WHERE YOU START.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then picture yourself the way a good friend might see you right now: tired, trying, doing your best with the day you've had. On each breath out, say quietly inside: may I be at ease. That's all. If it feels strange or even a little silly, that's normal. Say it anyway. The bell holds the time.
Kindness. Wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with the one in the mirror. Eighth word.
Your line: may I be at ease. Today, the next time you catch the harsh voice inside after a mistake, stop and ask what you'd say to a friend. Then say that to yourself. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THREE THINGS, OUT LOUD, BADLY.`

howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) meditation, practitioners often begin by silently wishing themselves well with a few short phrases, then extend the same wishes to a friend, a stranger, a difficult person and finally all beings.

original.note: Pali, from the Buddhist tradition: friendliness, loving-kindness. It comes from mitta, friend (Sanskrit maitrī).

trapdoor: what you thought: being nice to other people.
what it means: wanting good for someone the way a friend does, starting with yourself.
what a scholar hears: mettā, from mitta, friend; Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga (5th century) begins its practice with oneself before extending it outward.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (development of loving-kindness, beginning with oneself)
Kristin Neff, research on self-compassion (e.g. Neff 2003; Breines & Chen 2012)

notes: Mettā from mitta (friend): standard etymology; confirm.
Metta Sutta's mother-and-only-child image is paraphrased (Sutta Nipata 149).

Visuddhimagga IX: Buddhaghosa says to develop loving-kindness first toward oneself ('May I be happy and free from suffering'), then a dear person, a neutral person, a hostile person. 'About fifteen hundred years ago' dates him to the 5th century CE; confirm.
The Leviticus observation ('as thyself' assumes some care for oneself) is framed as a reader's observation, not a Jewish teaching; a Jewish Keeper may want to review.
Self-compassion findings (e.g. Breines & Chen 2012: self-compassion increased motivation to improve after failure) are summarized loosely; confirm wording 'tends to go the other way'.
Practice words 'may I be at ease' are a traditional-style metta phrase given as the day's carry, not a new prayer.
